subject: Public health
summary: Community health focuses on population-level interventions to prevent disease and promote health. It integrates surveillance, education, and primary care to address social determinants and reduce health inequities.

sections.p: Community health is the science and practice of improving health outcomes for groups through organized interventions, surveillance, and policy. Diagnosis is the identification of health problems at the population level using epidemiologic data and community assessments.
Severity is graded by burden of disease, morbidity, mortality, and inequity. Staging uses metrics like Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) and the Global Burden of Disease framework.

Root causes are social determinants: poverty, education, environment, and access to care. Biological factors include infectious agents (TB, malaria), chronic diseases (diabetes), and emerging threats (antimicrobial resistance).

t.b: High prevalence of anemia indicates nutritional deficiencies

sections.p: Community health problems manifest as clusters of illness, reduced life expectancy, and inequitable service access. Indicators include high infant mortality, vaccine gaps, and disease outbreaks.
Investigation relies on surveillance data, demographic health surveys, and sentinel site monitoring. Key tools are morbidity/mortality registries, GIS mapping, and rapid diagnostic tests.

t.b: Positive result triggers treatment and vector control

sections.p: Red flags include sudden increases in disease incidence, outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases, and deteriorating maternal health indicators.
Management integrates primary care, community health workers, and policy interventions. Strategies include health education, vaccination campaigns, vector control, and strengthening referral systems.

sections.p: Follow-up involves monitoring health indicators, evaluating program impact, and adjusting interventions. Prevention focuses on health promotion, disease surveillance, and equitable access to care.
b: Policy advocacy for universal health coverage

sections.p: Community health is often mistaken for public health, which is broader, or for primary care, which is individual-focused. It is distinct in its population-level focus and preventive orientation.
Surveillance data may underreport due to limited testing, and self-reported surveys can be biased. Low-resource settings may lack laboratory confirmation, leading to misclassification.

Self-reported vaccination status may overestimate coverage

faq.q: What is the main goal of community health?
faq.a: To improve health outcomes for populations through prevention, education, and equitable access to care.

faq.q: How do community health workers contribute?
faq.a: They provide culturally appropriate health education, basic services, and link patients to higher-level care.
It detects disease trends early, guiding timely interventions and resource allocation.
